subtopic_detail: Post-UTI imaging cascade after typical first UTI
stem:
A 14-month-old girl completed a 3 day course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a first febrile urinary tract infection two weeks ago. Urine culture from a clean catch specimen grew Escherichia coli at greater than 10 to the 8 CFU per litre, sensitive to the antibiotic used. Fever settled within 36 hours and she has been well since.

Antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal and postnatal renal function has never been checked. She had a normal newborn examination and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. She is up to date with immunisations, growing along the 50th centile for weight and length, and toilet training is not yet established. There have been no further urinary symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with no palpable masses, external genitalia normal, back and spine unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that imaging is not required and give safety-netting advice for future febrile illnesses
Arrange outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks with paediatric review of the imaging result
Arrange dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning at 4 to 6 months post-illness to assess for cortical scarring
Arrange micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux as an underlying cause
Commence low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg nocte for 12 months with paediatric clinic review

stem:
A 5-year-old boy weighing 22 kg attends a general practice for review after his second episode of anaphylaxis to cashew nut, this time triggered by an accidental exposure at kindergarten. On the first exposure two months ago he developed urticaria, lip swelling and audible wheeze that resolved with intramuscular adrenaline administered by paramedics.

Skin prick testing performed by an allergist has confirmed cashew and pistachio sensitisation with wheal sizes above the diagnostic cut-off. He has no other atopic disease, takes no regular medication, and there is no personal or family history of arrhythmia. Both parents have completed ASCIA anaphylaxis first aid training and are able to demonstrate correct injector technique on a trainer device.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: unremarkable

lead_in: Which adrenaline autoinjector prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
Two adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
A single adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and referral to community pharmacy for a second on request
A prescription for oral cetirizine 10 mg daily during pollen season with an adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector as required
A prescription for daily inhaled fluticasone 100 microgram twice daily and two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors

stem: A 3-year-old girl has had 4 days of crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea that has become visibly bloody. The family ate undercooked mince at a barbecue a week ago. She is alert, drinking well and passing urine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/60, RR 24, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild generalised tenderness, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Stool culture and polymerase chain reaction sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral rehydration and baseline bloods without antimicrobial cover
Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 3 days with oral rehydration
Oral trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole twice daily with oral rehydration
Oral loperamide 0.2 mg/kg with a low residue diet and oral rehydration
Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily until stool results return

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with 24 hours of fever, lethargy, and a non-blanching purpuric rash on the shins and buttocks that appeared this morning. He is now drowsy and difficult to rouse, cool peripherally to the mid-forearm, and has a prolonged capillary refill of 5 seconds at the sternum. He weighs 18 kg.

He is up to date with the National Immunisation Program schedule including meningococcal ACWY and B, and has no known allergies. His mother reports he was well enough to attend day care yesterday morning. He has no significant past medical history and is not on regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 168, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.8 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: After immediate airway assessment and application of monitoring, what is the correct order of the next four interventions?

options.text: Infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 minutes, obtain intravenous access afterwards, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
Commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
Draw a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
Obtain intravenous or intraosseous access, draw blood cultures, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, draw blood cultures, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus

stem:
A term female neonate born at 38 plus 4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery is reviewed on day 4 of life in the postnatal ward. Her mother is blood group O rhesus positive and the baby is A rhesus positive with a direct antiglobulin test negative and blood groups matched. She is exclusively breastfed with a 6 percent weight loss from birth and is otherwise well.

A transcutaneous bilirubin at 24 hours was 90 micromol/L. On clinical examination today at 96 hours of age she looks jaundiced to the mid-abdomen with normal tone, a strong cry, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Serum total bilirubin drawn is 320 micromol/L, predominantly unconjugated. Full blood count is unremarkable and reticulocyte count is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: total bilirubin 320 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 8 micromol/L, DAT negative, haemoglobin 175 g/L (150-220), reticulocyte count within normal limits, group and hold A rhesus positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an immediate double volume exchange transfusion after commencing intensive triple overhead phototherapy
Withhold breastfeeding for 48 hours, commence formula supplementation, and repeat the serum bilirubin level in 24 hours
Reassure the family that this represents physiological jaundice and arrange community midwife home review in 48 hours
Send urgent haemolysis screen including G6PD, pyruvate kinase and haemoglobin electrophoresis before starting treatment
Commence single overhead phototherapy, repeat the serum bilirubin in 6 hours, and continue breastfeeding with lactation support

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is reviewed in a paediatric assessment unit on day 6 of daily high fevers that have not responded to alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen. His parents describe non-purulent bilateral conjunctival redness that started on day 3, a strawberry appearance to his tongue since yesterday, and a rash on his trunk that has come and gone.

He has no cough, coryza, or diarrhoea. Blood tests today show a C-reactive protein of 90 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/hour, platelet count of 480 x10 to the 9 per litre, and mild sterile pyuria on urinalysis. Liver enzymes show an alanine aminotransferase of 90 U/L (less than 40). A recent throat swab for group A streptococcus is negative and there are no oral vesicles or exudate. There is no lymphadenopathy over 1.5 cm and no peripheral desquamation yet.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: CRP 90 mg/L (less than 5), ESR 60 mm/hour, platelets 480 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), ALT 90 U/L (less than 40), albumin 30 g/L (35-50), urinalysis with sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an urgent echocardiogram and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
Continue supportive care with paracetamol and reassess in 48 hours before considering any specific therapy
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin for suspected scarlet fever and repeat throat swab in 48 hours
Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as first-line monotherapy pending confirmation of coronary artery involvement
Arrange a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg for suspected meningitis

stem:
A 12-day-old term boy is brought to a rural emergency department at 3 a.m. by his parents who noticed poor feeding for the previous 24 hours and cool, mottled legs this morning. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, discharged at 24 hours after a normal newborn examination and passed the pre-discharge pulse oximetry screen with post-ductal saturation of 96 percent. He is exclusively breastfed and had been feeding well until yesterday.

On examination he is pale, grunting, and lethargic. The upper limbs are warm and pink; the lower limbs are cool and dusky. Right upper limb blood pressure is 88/48; right lower limb blood pressure is 40/22. There is a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a hyperdynamic praecordium. Femoral pulses are just palpable and delayed compared with the brachial pulses. Liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 176, blood pressure 88/48 right arm and 40/22 right leg, respiratory rate 68 with grunting, SpO2 pre-ductal 98 percent and post-ductal 90 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 5.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), chest x-ray with cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion, four-limb blood pressures with a 40 mmHg upper to lower limb gradient
data_table.Post-transfer arrangements: the nearest paediatric intensive care retrieval team has been contacted and estimated time of arrival is 90 minutes

lead_in: In addition to initial resuscitation, what is the single most important pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer an intravenous adenosine 100 microgram/kg rapid bolus for suspected supraventricular tachycardia
Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 nanograms/kg/minute after securing peripheral access
Commence an intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/minute as first-line vasoactive support
Administer an intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg bolus with fluid restriction for pulmonary venous congestion
Administer an intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg dose for empirical late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis

stem:
A 4-month-old former term infant presents to a tertiary paediatric ED in July with three days of coryza, worsening cough and feeding half his usual volume. He is alert but has moderate subcostal recessions and audible wheeze. Nasal swab PCR is positive for RSV.

His mother reports his lips looked slightly grey on the drive in, though they now look pink. He has never had wheeze before, was born at 39 weeks, and had no neonatal respiratory support.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 87% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mildly dehydrated, wet nappy 4 hours ago; widespread fine crackles with expiratory wheeze; no focal consolidation
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, pCO2 45 mmHg, HCO3 23 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: High-flow nasal cannulae at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 92%
Facemask oxygen at 6 L/min with SpO2 target 94 to 98 percent
Low-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to SpO2 90 percent
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with supplemental oxygen delivered via mask
Nebulised 3 percent hypertonic saline with room air observation off oxygen

stem:
A 20-month-old girl is brought to a regional ED at 2 am with a 24-hour history of coryza and a barking cough that started that evening. On arrival she has audible inspiratory stridor when upset but none at rest, and mild suprasternal tug when crying.

She settles quickly on her mother's lap and takes sips of juice. She has had no fever, no drooling and no cyanotic episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, playful when settled, barking cough on stimulation; chest clear apart from transmitted upper airway sounds; oropharynx normal
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed; clinical Westley score 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose?

options.text: Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily for three days as a course
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg orally as a single dose observed in ED
Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg orally as a single dose then discharge
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once with observation for two hours
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with 3 hours observation

stem: A 13-month-old boy had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. His vomiting settled, but he passes frequent explosive watery stools each time he drinks his usual cow milk formula. He is thriving and playful.

data_table.Examination: Perianal excoriation, soft abdomen, weight stable on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Stool pH 5.0 with positive reducing substances

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a lactose free formula and review in two weeks
Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review in two weeks
Start oral metronidazole and review the stools in two weeks
Start a soy based formula and refer for allergy testing
Continue the usual formula and refer for a coeliac screen

stem:
A 3-year-old boy weighing 15 kg presents to a GP clinic after eating a cashew biscuit at daycare. Ten minutes later he developed generalised urticaria, then hoarse voice and now audible stridor.

His mother had brought his previously prescribed EpiPen Jr for daycare use but has not administered it. He has been alert throughout but is becoming agitated. He is a known cashew-sensitised child with previous mild reactions but no prior anaphylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but agitated; generalised urticaria; audible stridor; increased work of breathing; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: No time for investigations; call for ambulance already made

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate adrenaline dose?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms via EpiPen Jr into anterolateral thigh
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms via EpiPen into anterolateral thigh
Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg diluted and titrated to response
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow facemask oxygen
Intramuscular adrenaline 75 micrograms drawn from ampoule based on weight

subtopic_detail: Extent of the sepsis evaluation in a febrile infant under three months with clinical bronchiolitis
stem: A 7-week-old boy born at term has had coryza and a cough for two days and now a fever. He is taking about three-quarters of his usual feeds and has had four wet nappies today.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4, HR 152, RR 52, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and well perfused; widespread wheeze and fine crackles; fontanelle soft; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send a catheter urine specimen and observe him without antibiotics
Perform a full septic screen with lumbar puncture and start antibiotics
Take a blood culture and start intravenous antibiotics without a screen
Start oral amoxicillin and review him in the community tomorrow morning
Discharge him with feeding advice and no further investigation today

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid rate and cerebral oedema risk
stem:
A 7-year-old girl weighing 22 kg presents with a two-day history of polyuria and polydipsia and today, vomiting and drowsiness. She has newly diagnosed diabetes based on a random glucose of 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 6.1 mmol/L, and venous pH 7.10.

Her initial GCS was 14 (E3 V5 M6) on arrival and she has received a single 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes. Sodium is 132 mmol/L and corrected sodium is 141 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is 6 mmol/L. She has just been re-examined 30 minutes after the bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min (Kussmaul), SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils equal 3 mm reactive, mildly complaining of headache; abdomen soft, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 27 mmol/L, ketones 6.1 mmol/L, pH 7.11, HCO3 6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (corrected 141), potassium 4.9 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give another 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes and continue rehydration
Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 15 minutes and reduce fluid rate to maintenance
Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately to reverse ongoing ketosis
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 60 minutes to correct the metabolic acidosis
Change intravenous fluid to 0.45 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent glucose over the next hour

stem:
A 14-month-old girl presented four days ago with fever, foul-smelling urine and a positive catheter urine culture growing more than 10^8 CFU/L of Escherichia coli fully sensitive to trimethoprim. She was commenced on oral trimethoprim and has been afebrile within 36 hours.

Antenatal ultrasounds at 20 and 32 weeks gestation were normal. She has been feeding normally, growing along her expected centile, and has had no prior urinary tract infections. Her mother asks what imaging her daughter now needs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well hydrated, playful; abdomen soft with no palpable masses; genitalia normal appearing
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim; creatinine 32 micromol/L (within paediatric range); resolution of fever within 36 hours of therapy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan now?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during this illness within 48 hours of admission
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) at completion of antibiotic course
No imaging indicated; safety net advice for recurrent urinary symptoms only
DMSA renal cortical scan at four to six months to assess renal scarring
Renal tract ultrasound routinely at four to six weeks post infection

stem:
A 3-year-old boy has had a fever above 39 degrees for 6 days despite 48 hours of oral amoxicillin. His parents report cracked red lips, red eyes without pus, and a fine truncal rash that comes and goes. On examination he is irritable but not toxic, with a single 20 mm right anterior cervical node. Palms and soles are not swollen or peeling. Throat swab for group A streptococcus and blood culture are negative.

He has no household exposure to measles, no travel history and is fully immunised. The ED registrar has already arranged a formal echocardiogram, which shows a left anterior descending coronary artery Z score of +2.7.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cracked lips, bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection, polymorphous truncal rash, single 20 mm right anterior cervical node; hands and feet not swollen; no BCG scar reaction
data_table.Investigations: CRP 142 mg/L (<5), ESR 74 mm/hr, WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (5-15), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-450), ALT 78 U/L (<40), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), sterile pyuria 40 leucocytes/HPF; blood culture and throat swab negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IVIG 2 g/kg intravenously over 10 hours together with high dose aspirin
Await the fifth principal clinical feature before starting definitive therapy
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as sole first-line anti-inflammatory therapy
Escalate to intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed occult bacterial infection
Discharge with 48-hour ambulatory review and antipyretic advice at home

stem:
A term female infant born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks is reviewed on the postnatal ward at 28 hours of age because she looks yellow to the midwife. Her mother is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen; the baby's cord blood group is A positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. Birthweight was 3.4 kg, she is breastfeeding on demand and has passed meconium and urine.

She is alert, feeding well, has moist mucous membranes and normal tone. There is no cephalohaematoma and no significant bruising.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, jaundice to the chest, no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae; feeding effectively at breast
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 260 micromol/L (unconjugated); haemoglobin 165 g/L (140-220); reticulocytes 6 percent (2-6); blood film unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase breastfeeding frequency and reassess bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours
Start intensive phototherapy now and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours
Arrange immediate double volume exchange transfusion in the neonatal unit
Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin one gram per kilogram now
Formula supplementation only with recheck of bilirubin the following morning

stem:
A previously well 5-month-old boy is admitted with a first febrile urinary tract infection. Suprapubic aspirate grew pure Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin. He responded within 24 hours to intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and is now afebrile, feeding well and passing clear urine. A routine antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks documented normal renal tract anatomy, and he is thriving on the 50th centile.

He has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. The ED consultant asks whether imaging is required before discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused; abdomen soft with no mass; genitalia normal circumcised; no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Suprapubic aspirate urine: pure Escherichia coli >10^8 CFU/L, sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin; creatinine 32 micromol/L; normal antenatal renal tract ultrasound at 20 weeks

lead_in: What imaging strategy is most appropriate before discharge?

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram planned once the acute illness has resolved
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to detect renal cortical scarring reliably
No renal tract imaging is indicated as antenatal ultrasound was normal
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks of resolution in the community
Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography before discharge from hospital

stem:
A 6-year-old girl presented three weeks ago with a palpable purpuric rash on the buttocks and lower limbs, right knee arthritis and colicky abdominal pain. Skin biopsy at that admission showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis and she was managed with paracetamol and outpatient follow-up. Symptoms have fully resolved. Blood pressure was normal throughout admission and initial urine dipstick was clear.

She returns for the planned review. Her mother reports she has been well, eating normally and returned to school. The GP has done no interval investigations since discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no residual rash or joint swelling; abdomen soft; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Today: urine dipstick trace protein, no blood; formal urine protein/creatinine ratio pending; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Discharge from follow-up as the acute illness has resolved without complication
Renal biopsy this week to detect and characterise late-onset HSP nephritis
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks to prevent renal complications
Weekly BP and urine dipstick surveillance for 6 months from initial presentation
Immediate nephrology referral for consideration of ACE inhibitor prophylaxis

stem:
A 14-year-old girl attends the general paediatric clinic with a 12-month history of migraine without aura. She now has 6 attacks per month, each lasting most of a day, and has missed 4 days of school in the last month. Simple analgesics are effective when taken early, and she has responded to oral sumatriptan on 3 occasions. Her diary shows no clear food triggers, sleep is regular, and she is not on any hormonal contraception.

Mother describes similar migraines through her own adolescence. Neurological examination and fundoscopy today are normal, blood pressure is normal for her age and weight is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination and fundoscopy within normal limits; no papilloedema; no meningism; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Headache diary confirms 6 attacks per month over 3 months; MRI brain not indicated on clinical features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic strategy?

options.text: Start oral propranolol 10 mg twice daily and review response at 8 weeks
Start oral topiramate 25 mg nightly and titrate slowly to a target 100 mg daily
Start oral amitriptyline 10 mg nightly and review response at 8 weeks in clinic
Start rizatriptan 5 mg regularly at bedtime nightly as an oral prophylactic
Arrange urgent MRI brain with contrast for further diagnostic assessment

subtopic_detail: Positive newborn screen for cystic fibrosis
stem:
A 3-week-old boy is referred urgently by the state newborn screening service. His day 3 immunoreactive trypsinogen was elevated, and second-tier CFTR gene analysis identified two variants: F508del in trans with R117H-7T. He is his parents' first child, weight is on the 50th centile, and he has been feeding well with normal wet nappies and passing stool.

Both parents are white European. The parents are anxious after receiving the phone call the same morning and want to know what will confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused; chest clear; abdomen soft; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: NBS: IRT elevated day 3; CFTR analysis F508del/R117H-7T; family history negative for CF

lead_in: What is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Repeat immunoreactive trypsinogen level at 6 weeks of age in the community
Sweat chloride test performed once the infant weighs 3 kilograms or more
Faecal elastase measurement to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
Nasal potential difference measurement at the tertiary respiratory service
High resolution CT chest to detect early structural bronchiectasis at baseline

stem:
A 5-year-old boy has 12 months of infrequent bowel motions (once every 4 to 5 days) with increasing daily soiling in his underwear over the last 3 months. He complains of tummy pain that is relieved by passing stool. His mother is embarrassed and stressed because his prep teacher has raised concerns. Diet includes little fruit, adequate fibre otherwise, and he drinks 1 litre of water daily.

He grew normally, has no perianal fissure and no red flags for organic disease. There is no delayed passage of meconium, no family history of Hirschsprung disease. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well; abdomen soft with a palpable indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa; perianal area normal without fissure; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: None; clinical diagnosis of functional constipation with overflow soiling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Behavioural toileting program alone with review in six weeks in general practice
Increase dietary fibre and daily fluid intake with a review in four weeks by GP
Oral macrogol disimpaction protocol titrating dose over 3 to 7 days as tolerated
Rectal phosphate enema now in ED followed by discharge on oral maintenance
Manual disimpaction under general anaesthetic in the paediatric surgery day list

stem:
A 20-month-old girl attends general paediatric outpatients with a 3-month history of pallor and reduced energy. She drinks 900 mL of cow's milk a day, eats a limited solid food range and has never accepted red meat. Her weight is on the 25th centile and unchanged from 6 months ago. Blood tests were done in the community 2 weeks ago.

First-line oral iron polymaltose was tried for 2 weeks by her GP; she refused every dose and vomited twice. There is no family history of iron malabsorption, coeliac serology is negative and her mother's antenatal ferritin was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no scleral icterus; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (105-135), MCV 62 fL (75-87), ferritin 6 microgram/L (30-300), CRP 3 mg/L (<5); coeliac serology and faecal occult blood negative; reticulocyte count reduced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Continue oral iron polymaltose 6 mg/kg elemental iron daily for 3 more months
Switch to a different oral iron formulation and repeat FBC in 4 weeks
Blood transfusion in day unit with subsequent oral iron maintenance therapy
Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion in the paediatric day medical unit
Reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL daily and review haemoglobin in three months

stem:
An 11-year-old girl is admitted from clinic with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and 3 kg unintentional weight loss. Random venous glucose in the surgery was 22 mmol/L. She is alert, warm and well-perfused with normal breathing. Ketones are 1.4 mmol/L on capillary meter and venous blood gas shows pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L. GAD antibodies are pending.

She is otherwise well, on no medications, and eats a mixed carbohydrate diet with 3 main meals and 2 snacks. There is no family history of type 1 diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-hydrated; no Kussmaul breathing; abdomen soft; no acanthosis nigricans
data_table.Investigations: Venous glucose 22 mmol/L; capillary ketones 1.4 mmol/L; venous gas pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L; HbA1c 11.2 percent; U and E within normal limits; weight 34 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial insulin regimen?

options.text: Continuous intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with hourly BSL
Basal insulin degludec once daily only with no meal-time boluses initially
Twice daily premixed 70/30 insulin with dose split before breakfast and dinner
Subcutaneous basal-bolus regimen with glargine and rapid-acting insulin at meals
Oral metformin 500 mg twice daily and repeat testing in 6 weeks in clinic

stem:
A 5-day-old term male infant is transferred from a peripheral hospital because of ongoing hypoglycaemia despite frequent breast feeds and formula top-ups every 3 hours. Birthweight was 4.2 kg and delivery was uncomplicated; mother was screened GDM-negative. The lowest recorded blood glucose has been 1.6 mmol/L, occurring 60 minutes after a feed. Between feeds he is jittery and this settles with feeding.

He is alert, has good tone and no dysmorphic features. There is no birth trauma, cephalohaematoma or midline defect. Free T4 is normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 144/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; large for gestational age; no dysmorphism; no midline cleft; genitalia normal; anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 1.6 mmol/L; cortisol, growth hormone, insulin, C-peptide, ammonia, lactate, urine ketones sample sent during hypoglycaemia; free T4 normal for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?

options.text: Send a critical sample for insulin and cortisol at the next hypoglycaemic event
Empirical intramuscular glucagon 0.5 mg for suspected persistent hyperinsulinism
Immediate MRI head and pituitary before hypoglycaemia is corrected in ED
Trial of diazoxide 5 mg/kg per day orally before formal biochemistry results
Chromosomal microarray to detect Beckwith-Wiedemann related hyperinsulinism

stem:
A 6-year-old girl weighing 22 kg had biphasic anaphylaxis 4 hours ago after accidental cashew ingestion at a birthday party. She received 300 microgram intramuscular adrenaline at the first symptom onset with rapid resolution, and a second 300 microgram dose 3 hours later when hoarseness, wheeze and hypotension recurred. She has again responded fully and vital signs are normal.

She has a documented cashew allergy and carries her own EpiPen. She has no asthma and no previous ICU admissions. Both parents are present, competent and speak English fluently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, no rash currently; chest clear with no wheeze; oropharynx normal; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: No acute investigations required beyond clinical monitoring; ECG unremarkable

lead_in: What is the minimum appropriate observation period from the second adrenaline dose?

options.text: Two hours of observation because response to the second dose has been complete
Four hours after the second adrenaline dose provided the child remains stable
Twelve hours of hospital observation because of biphasic pattern and second dose
Twenty-four hours of admission and paediatric high dependency unit review
Forty-eight hours of admission because of confirmed food-triggered anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotics for meningitis in a young infant
stem:
A 6-week-old former term boy is brought to a regional ED with 12 hours of fever, poor feeding and increasing irritability. He is difficult to console, has a full anterior fontanelle and mottled peripheries. Capillary refill centrally is 3 seconds. Bloods and lumbar puncture have been obtained without difficulty and blood culture is drawn.

He is exclusively breastfed, has had all birth screening, and has no known immunodeficiency. His parents are Australian and there is no unusual travel or contact history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176/min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but inconsolable; full anterior fontanelle; mottled peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds centrally; no rash
data_table.Investigations: CSF: WCC 480/mm3 (85 percent neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 1.6 mmol/L with plasma 5.4 mmol/L; Gram stain negative; blood culture drawn; WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg daily as sole empirical antimicrobial therapy
Intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours and gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily
Intravenous vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 6 hours as monotherapy for CSF cover
Intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 6 hours and amoxicillin 50 mg/kg every 6 hours
Cefotaxime 50 mg/kg 6-hourly, amoxicillin 50 mg/kg 6-hourly plus dexamethasone

stem:
A 4-year-old boy on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia was in the same primary school classroom as another child who developed a chickenpox rash yesterday. His medical team confirms he received VZV vaccination pre-diagnosis but has not had chickenpox. He has been on maintenance chemotherapy for 8 months and his most recent lymphocyte count was 0.6 x10^9/L. Contact occurred 20 hours ago in an indoor setting for over an hour.

He is currently well with no fever, malaise or rash. His mother contacted the oncology fellow this morning to ask what to do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 100/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well; no rash; oropharynx clear; abdomen soft; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Absolute lymphocyte count 0.6 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0); recent varicella IgG antibody titre pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure management?

options.text: Zoster immunoglobulin (ZIG) intramuscular within 96 hours of contact today
Give the varicella live-attenuated vaccine within 5 days of the contact today
Start oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg 4 times daily for 7 days immediately as prophylaxis
No action; the vaccine received before diagnosis provides adequate ongoing protection
Admit today for intravenous immunoglobulin and prolonged inpatient monitoring

stem: A 4-month-old girl with bronchiolitis is too tachypnoeic to feed safely and has vomited her nasogastric feeds twice. She weighs 6 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 68, SpO2 92 percent on 1 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Moderate recession, moist mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intravenous fluid prescription?

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9 percent with glucose at two thirds maintenance
Sodium chloride 0.45 percent with glucose at the full maintenance rate
Sodium chloride 0.9 percent with glucose at full maintenance rate
Glucose 5 percent alone at two thirds of the maintenance rate
Sodium chloride 0.9 percent as a 20 mL/kg bolus then maintenance

stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department at midnight with a barking cough and hoarse voice for 6 hours. She has a mild coryzal illness for 2 days. She is fully immunised, was born at term with no neonatal issues and has never previously been hospitalised.

On arrival she is alert, sitting comfortably in her father's arms and has an audible barking cough with intermittent inspiratory stridor when upset. Between episodes of crying she has no stridor at rest and mild suprasternal recession only when distressed. She accepts a sip of water.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure not measured, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, barking cough on examination; stridor with crying only; no drooling; chest clear to auscultation between coughs
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first steroid dose?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once now and reassess after 2 hours
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once now and observe for at least 30 minutes
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg once now and admit for overnight monitoring
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg once and discharge home after 15 minutes of observation
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with no steroid until stridor at rest returns

stem:
A 22-month-old boy presents with 24 hours of watery non-bloody diarrhoea (six loose stools today) and three episodes of non-bilious vomiting. He weighs 12 kg. His mother reports reduced but not absent oral intake and one wet nappy in the past 8 hours. There has been no fever, no rash and no unwell contacts other than a similar mild illness in his older sibling.

On arrival he is clingy but consolable, has slightly dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor over the abdomen. Capillary refill is 2 seconds centrally, extremities are warm. He gags on the first oral rehydration sip and vomits it back within 5 minutes despite a small volume.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mildly dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 seconds central; abdomen soft, non-tender; no rash; weight 12 kg (usual 12.4 kg)
data_table.Investigations: No routine bloods indicated at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Admit for IV maintenance fluids alone without any enteral rehydration attempt
Insert an IV cannula and give 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 20 minutes now
Insert a nasogastric tube and give oral rehydration solution at 20 mL/kg over 1 hour
Discharge home with advice to offer small frequent oral fluids and review in 4 hours
Give a single oral ondansetron 4 mg and repeat oral rehydration attempt after 20 minutes

subtopic_detail: Fluid bolus volume in a shocked febrile infant under three months
stem: A 3-week-old girl is brought in with poor feeding and lethargy. She is mottled with a capillary refill of four seconds. You have intravenous access and blood cultures have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6, HR 192, RR 62, BP 58/32, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L, venous lactate 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg, then reassess
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg, then reassess
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 40 mL/kg, then reassess
Intravenous 4% albumin 20 mL/kg, then reassess perfusion
Intravenous 10% glucose 5 mL/kg, then reassess perfusion

stem:
A 3-year-old girl presents with 12 hours of fever, lethargy and a non-blanching rash on her legs that has spread to her trunk over the past hour. She has been unwell since yesterday with 24 hours of vomiting and reduced oral intake. She is fully immunised and previously well. Her weight is 15 kg.

On arrival she is drowsy but rouseable, has cool peripheries, capillary refill of 4 seconds centrally and a non-blanching purpuric rash on her lower limbs and abdomen. Her SpO2 is 96 percent on room air and she has no stridor, wheeze or focal chest signs. Point-of-care lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, blood pressure 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rouseable; capillary refill 4 seconds central; cool peripheries; non-blanching rash on lower limbs and abdomen; no meningism yet
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care lactate 4.2 mmol/L; venous access not yet obtained

lead_in: What is the correct order for the first three resuscitation actions?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, then take blood cultures, then give antibiotics
Start adrenaline infusion first, then obtain access and then give antibiotics after fluids
Perform lumbar puncture immediately for CSF then give antibiotics tailored to CSF findings
Intubate first for airway protection then obtain access and give antibiotics after airway is secured
Obtain IV or intraosseous access, take blood cultures, then give first IV antibiotic within the hour

subtopic_detail: UTI imaging pathway in a toddler
stem:
A 20-month-old girl is brought to your general practice for review one week after her first confirmed urinary tract infection. She had 48 hours of fever and irritability, urine culture grew Escherichia coli with clean-catch collection, and she was treated with 5 days of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She defervesced within 36 hours of starting antibiotics.

She is now clinically well with normal feeding and activity. She had an unremarkable antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks that documented normal kidneys and bladder. She has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, no palpable abdominal mass on examination today, and no growth concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure not routinely measured, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and active; abdomen soft with no palpable mass; genitalia normal; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture from admission grew E coli fully sensitive; renal function during illness within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No routine imaging required now; safety-net for recurrence and any atypical features later
Micturating cystourethrogram within 4 weeks to identify any vesicoureteric reflux
Start daily prophylactic trimethoprim for 6 months and re-image only if breakthrough occurs
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks and a follow-up ultrasound at 12 months routinely
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA scan at 6 months regardless of ultrasound findings

subtopic_detail: Anaphylaxis IM adrenaline in a marginal-weight child
stem:
A 5-year-old girl with a known peanut allergy is brought to your remote clinic 15 minutes after biting into a satay skewer at a family barbecue. She has developed a widespread urticarial rash, hoarse voice, one episode of vomiting and audible wheeze. Her mother reports she weighs approximately 19 kg (recent GP weight was 18.6 kg). She has no other medical history and takes no regular medications.

On arrival she is anxious with visible tongue swelling and audible bilateral wheeze. She has a soft stridor at rest and is starting to look pale. Your clinic stocks the current PBS anaphylaxis kits: EpiPen Jr 150 microgram autoinjector and EpiPen 300 microgram autoinjector, plus 1 mg/mL adrenaline ampoules and 1 mL syringes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 82/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Tongue swelling, urticarial rash, wheeze bilaterally, stridor at rest, pale peripheries; alert but anxious
data_table.Investigations: Weight documented as 18.6 kg 4 weeks ago; mother estimates 19 kg today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first adrenaline dose to give right now?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 microgram intravenous bolus after establishing IV access first
Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscular via EpiPen Jr autoinjector into the mid outer thigh
Adrenaline 190 microgram intramuscular calculated as 10 microgram per kg from the ampoule
Adrenaline 300 microgram intramuscular via EpiPen autoinjector into the mid outer thigh
Adrenaline 500 microgram intramuscular drawn from a 1 mg per mL ampoule now

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid strategy with cerebral oedema risk factors
stem:
A 9-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents to your tertiary paediatric emergency after 24 hours of Kussmaul breathing, vomiting and progressive drowsiness. She weighs 28 kg. She was well until 3 weeks ago when polyuria and 4 kg weight loss began. On arrival she is drowsy but obeys commands intermittently (GCS 13), has deep sighing respiration and warm dry skin. Her mother reports she has become more confused in the last hour of transport.

Her arterial blood gas shows pH 6.98, bicarbonate 4 mmol/L, glucose 34 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, corrected sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, and ketones 6.2 mmol/L. She has not yet received IV fluids or insulin. Her intravenous cannula is in situ and blood cultures are drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min deep, SpO2 100 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; Kussmaul breathing; warm dry skin; capillary refill 3 seconds central; no focal neurology; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: pH 6.98; HCO3 4 mmol/L (22-32); glucose 34 mmol/L (3.5-7.7); Na 128 mmol/L (135-145) corrected 133; K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); ketones 6.2 mmol/L; weight 28 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Withhold all IV fluid until insulin infusion has run for 1 hour to observe glucose trend first with routine outpatient follow-up
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin every 2 hours titrated to point-of-care glucose without any IV insulin as the sole intervention
10 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 30 minutes then start maintenance plus replacement calculated over 48 hours; insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour
20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 20 minutes twice then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately as the sole intervention
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the pH before any insulin is given with routine outpatient follow-up

stem:
A 4-month-old boy presents to your emergency department with two days of coryza followed by increased work of breathing overnight. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, is exclusively breastfed and has taken about half his usual feeds today. He has had no fever above 38 degrees C at home. There is no family history of asthma.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms with visible subcostal recession, occasional expiratory wheeze and widespread fine crackles bilaterally. Capillary refill is under two seconds. A nasopharyngeal viral swab is positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Nursing staff have placed him on low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute, with SpO2 now stable at 91 percent, and he has managed a further breastfeed since arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158/min, blood pressure 90/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 58/min, SpO2 91 percent on 1 L/min nasal prong, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, subcostal recession, mild tracheal tug, widespread expiratory wheeze and fine crackles
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; capillary blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 46 mmHg, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing respiratory support plan?

options.text: Continue low-flow nasal prong oxygen, re-assess in two hours, and only escalate to high-flow nasal cannula if this fails
Switch immediately to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min because low-flow oxygen is inadequate in RSV bronchiolitis
Aim for SpO2 above 94 percent by titrating oxygen upward on the current nasal prong device
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg alongside oxygen while planning any escalation of respiratory support
Cease supplemental oxygen and observe on room air since the current SpO2 is above the accepted target

stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to your regional emergency department by her father at 2 am with a barky cough and hoarse voice for six hours. She had a runny nose the day before but no fever above 38 degrees C, no drooling and no history of choking. She has had no previous episodes and is fully immunised. Her weight today is 12 kg.

On assessment she is alert, sitting in her father's lap and interacting. She has audible stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession at rest and no cyanosis. Air entry is equal bilaterally with no wheeze. She has taken sips of water without difficulty. There is no obvious lymphadenopathy. She has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Barky cough, hoarse voice, stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession, no drooling, no accessory muscle use at rest
data_table.Investigations: Not required for typical croup

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dosing plan now?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 solution alone and observe for a further four hours without oral steroid
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kilogram as a single dose with discharge planning after observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram as a single dose with admission for at least six hours of observation
Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram once daily for three days as an equivalent alternative to dexamethasone
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kilogram given together for additive airway effect

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months full septic workup
stem:
A 6-week-old term boy is brought to your metropolitan emergency department by his parents after a measured axillary temperature of 38.4 degrees C at home. He is exclusively breastfed. Over the last twelve hours he has become sleepier than usual with feeds shorter than his previous pattern and one episode of non-bilious vomiting after a feed. There has been no diarrhoea and his wet nappy count is reduced from ten to six today.

On arrival he is pale but rousable, with mild tachycardia and cool peripheries. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no rash and no focal source on examination. Capillary refill centrally is three seconds. Weight is on the 25th percentile and has fallen from the 50th on the growth chart since his six-week check. He has never had a septic workup.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, sleepy but rousable, cool peripheries, soft fontanelle, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care venous glucose 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); capillary lactate 3.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); urine dipstick pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management pathway?

options.text: Send a bagged urine specimen and observe on the ward for six hours before deciding about further investigations
Take blood cultures, start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin, and defer the lumbar puncture until the child is more stable
Perform full septic workup including catheter urine, blood cultures and lumbar puncture, then give empirical intravenous cefotaxime
Give a single dose of oral paracetamol 15 mg per kilogram and reassess response over the next hour before further tests
Request a same-day outpatient viral polymerase chain reaction panel and discharge home with a red flag advice sheet

stem:
An 18-month-old girl presents to your paediatric emergency department with 24 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea and three episodes of vomiting. She has had four wet nappies in the last day compared with her usual eight, but is still passing some urine. She lives in inner Melbourne and had no recent travel or antibiotic use. Her weight today is 11 kg; the family baby scale two weeks ago recorded 11.6 kg.

On examination she is fussy but drinks small sips when offered, has slightly dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes and reduced skin turgor. Capillary refill is two seconds; she is not tachypnoeic. She has already refused an oral rehydration solution trial in triage, spitting most sips out. Her venous glucose is normal. A single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg was well tolerated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 140/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.3 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fussy but consolable, slightly dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill two seconds
data_table.Investigations: Venous glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); venous blood gas within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration route now?

options.text: Continue small volume oral rehydration attempts at the bedside every ten minutes and reassess in four hours
Establish intravenous access and give a 20 mL per kilogram bolus of normal saline over 20 minutes as first-line rehydration
Give intramuscular ondansetron 0.15 mg per kilogram and observe for further improvement over the next two hours
Pass a nasogastric tube and rehydrate with oral rehydration solution over 4 to 6 hours as first-line for failed oral intake
Commence half normal saline with 5 percent dextrose at 1.5 times maintenance rate intravenously without a bolus

subtopic_detail: Late onset neonatal sepsis with disconfirming feature
stem:
A term day 8 boy is brought to your regional emergency department by his mother for poor feeding and one episode of grunting in the last two hours. He was born at 40 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth after a term pregnancy with group B streptococcus negative screen and no maternal fever. His mother has felt well throughout. He has been mixed-fed for the last five days after her supply concerns.

On arrival he is pale and quiet, with a soft anterior fontanelle, mildly reduced tone and no rash. Capillary refill is three seconds and peripheries are cool. His axillary temperature is 35.6 degrees C. Blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5). Careful examination reveals scaphoid abdomen and reduced femoral pulses relative to brachial pulses; four-limb blood pressures show right arm 74/44 mmHg and right leg 44/28 mmHg. Chest is clear with an accentuated second heart sound and no murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176/min, blood pressure right arm 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min with grunting, SpO2 88 percent right arm 78 percent leg on room air, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, quiet, reduced tone, soft fontanelle, no rash, scaphoid abdomen, femoral pulses weak compared with brachial, pre-post ductal SpO2 differential
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.24, lactate 6.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), base excess -9; venous glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); CRP 4 mg/L (<10)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial intervention?

options.text: Take blood cultures then give intravenous amoxicillin and gentamicin empirically for late-onset neonatal sepsis
Give a 20 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus over 20 minutes before further reassessment
Intubate immediately and hyperventilate to a target pCO2 of 30 mmHg to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance
Administer intramuscular vitamin K 1 mg and correct the hypoglycaemia with an oral feed before further planning
Start intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion and arrange urgent retrieval to a paediatric cardiac centre

stem:
A 9-month-old boy is transferred to your tertiary paediatric ward on day 6 of persistent fever. His parents describe daily temperatures above 39 degrees C, unresponsive to alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has been miserable and off his feeds. Two urine cultures have grown mixed skin flora only and a chest radiograph was clear. Blood cultures at 48 hours are negative.

On examination he is irritable but consolable, with generalised maculopapular rash on the trunk that has come and gone, dry cracked lips and no conjunctival injection. There is a single 2 cm right anterior cervical lymph node and mild peripheral oedema of the hands but no obvious desquamation. Urea and electrolytes and liver enzymes are within normal limits apart from a rising albumin-corrected sodium in the low range. Recent bloods show haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 118 mg/L (<10), ESR 74 mm/h (<15) and albumin 26 g/L (32-45). Echocardiography today shows a coronary artery Z score of +2.7 in the left anterior descending artery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min, blood pressure 96/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Irritable, dry cracked lips, transient truncal maculopapular rash, 2 cm right cervical node, mild hand oedema, no conjunctival injection, no oral ulcers
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (105-135); platelets 620 x10^9/L (150-450); CRP 118 mg/L (<10); ESR 74 mm/h (<15); albumin 26 g/L (32-45); echocardiography LAD Z score +2.7

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate treatment plan today?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram single infusion plus high-dose aspirin
Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and cefotaxime while awaiting further cultures over the next 24 hours
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram daily as monotherapy for suspected autoinflammatory disease
Watchful waiting with paracetamol and ibuprofen and repeat the echocardiogram in 48 hours
Rheumatology referral for anakinra therapy without IVIG because coronary changes indicate IL-1 driven disease

subtopic_detail: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia oral iron
stem:
A 22-month-old girl presents to your general practice for a routine check because her mother is worried she is pale and less energetic than her older sibling was at the same age. She was born at term with an uncomplicated pregnancy and was breastfed until 11 months when she moved to cow's milk. She currently drinks around 900 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle and eats a mostly beige diet of pasta, bread and biscuits.

On examination she is alert and interactive; conjunctival pallor is noted and there is no jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Growth is on the 25th centile for weight and 50th for height, tracking her prior curve. She has no bruising. Her father is of Anglo-Australian background; her mother is of Italian background with no history of anaemia. Recent bloods show haemoglobin 88 g/L (105-135), mean cell volume 62 fL (75-87), mean cell haemoglobin 21 pg (25-33), reticulocytes 0.4 percent, ferritin 6 mcg/L (30-300) and transferrin saturation 6 percent. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (105-135); MCV 62 fL (75-87); MCH 21 pg (25-33); reticulocytes 0.4 percent; ferritin 6 mcg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 6 percent; haemoglobin electrophoresis normal for age; coeliac screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Refer for packed red cell transfusion because the haemoglobin is below 90 g/L in a symptomatic toddler
Start oral iron 3 mg per kilogram per day of elemental iron and cap cow's milk intake at 500 mL daily
Arrange intravenous iron polymaltose infusion under paediatric day-stay supervision this week
Trial a strictly gluten-free diet for eight weeks and repeat the full blood count without iron therapy
Give a single intramuscular iron dextran injection today and review in 6 weeks with a repeat full blood count

subtopic_detail: Constipation with red flags requiring investigation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-week-old boy in outpatients referred by his GP for infrequent stools since birth. He passed his first meconium at 52 hours after birth requiring digital stimulation, and he now opens his bowels every 4 to 7 days with small hard pellets that only pass after a rectal thermometer. He is exclusively breastfed on demand. His weight has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile since birth.

On examination his abdomen is visibly distended with palpable stool in the left iliac fossa. Rectal examination by the consultant reveals a tight anal sphincter with an empty rectum, followed by an explosive release of foul-smelling stool and gas as the finger is withdrawn. Perianal skin is intact with no fissures visible. There is no lower limb weakness and the anocutaneous reflex is present. He has never had bloody stools. Antenatal and perinatal courses were uneventful.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 42/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, palpable left iliac fossa stool, tight anal tone, empty rectum with explosive release on withdrawal of examining finger
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits; thyroid function tests pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trial two weeks of oral macrogol 3350 with review before considering any further investigation
Request abdominal ultrasound to assess for anatomical obstruction and mesenteric adenopathy
Refer to paediatric surgery for suction rectal biopsy to investigate for Hirschsprung disease
Order abdominal radiograph and start daily glycerol suppositories while awaiting the film report
Send stool for calprotectin and reducing substances to exclude inflammatory bowel disease

stem:
A 5-week-old exclusively breastfed boy is brought to your emergency department by his mother with a 6-hour history of poor feeding and one episode of blood-tinged vomit. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated home birth attended by a private midwife. His mother declined all injections after birth for her son, including vitamin K, on personal grounds. He has otherwise been well until this morning.

On examination he is pale and irritable but rousable. His anterior fontanelle is full and tense. There is bruising over the left flank without a history of trauma. His mucous membranes are pale and dry. There is no rash. Point-of-care venous glucose is 3.8 mmol/L (2.6 to 5.5). His mother has no personal or family bleeding disorder history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 174/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 50/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, irritable but rousable, tense anterior fontanelle, unexplained left flank bruise, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 74 g/L (105-135); platelets 260 x10^9/L (150-450); INR 5.8 (0.9-1.2); APTT 82 seconds (25-38); fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (1.5-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Give a single dose of oral vitamin K 2 mg with plans for repeat oral doses at 1 week and 6 weeks
Administer intravenous vitamin K 1 mg and transfuse fresh frozen plasma 10 to 20 mL per kilogram immediately
Give intravenous four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units per kilogram as sole therapy for the coagulopathy
Transfuse cryoprecipitate 5 mL per kilogram to correct suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation before further tests
Arrange non-contrast head computed tomography before any coagulation product to characterise the bleed first

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia oral iron dosing
stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to your general practice for a routine check by her mother. She drinks about 900 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle and eats limited solids. She has been pale for months but is otherwise well, meeting motor milestones and gaining weight along the 25th centile. There is no history of bleeding, prior surgery, or chronic diarrhoea, and she has never been transfused.

On examination she is pale but alert and playful. There is no jaundice, no hepatosplenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. Her heart sounds are dual with a soft flow murmur that disappears on standing. She has slightly spoon-shaped nails but no glossitis. Recent bloods show haemoglobin 82 g/L (110-140), MCV 66 fL (75-87), ferritin 6 microgram/L (12-150), and a normal reticulocyte count. Coeliac serology is negative and she has no blood in her stools.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, playful, soft flow murmur that resolves on standing, mild koilonychia, no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 82 g/L (110-140); MCV 66 fL (75-87); ferritin 6 mcg/L (12-150); reticulocytes normal; coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management plan?

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to no more than 500 mL daily and start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg per kilogram elemental iron once daily
Refer for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion because oral iron is unlikely to correct a haemoglobin below 90 g/L
Reduce cow's milk to no more than 500 mL daily, start oral ferrous sulfate 3 to 6 mg per kilogram elemental iron daily and recheck the FBC in 4 to 6 weeks
Recommend dietary iron enrichment alone and repeat the full blood count in 3 months without pharmacological iron replacement
Transfuse packed red blood cells 10 mL per kilogram now to raise the haemoglobin above 90 g/L before dietary changes

stem:
A 6-week-old term boy is brought to your metropolitan emergency department after a single episode in his cot 90 minutes ago. His mother heard a choking noise, found him limp and cyanotic around the mouth, gently repositioned him and he pinked up and cried within 20 to 30 seconds. He has fed normally since and slept in her arms in the waiting room. He was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, is exclusively breastfed and is on no medications. There has been no coryza, no fever and no vomiting.

On examination he is alert, feeding vigorously and interactive. Anterior fontanelle is soft; there is no bruising, no rash and no dysmorphism. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are unremarkable. Point-of-care venous glucose is 4.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5). His growth is on the 50th centile and his mother has no smoking history. No family member has died suddenly in infancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 90/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 38/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeding well, no bruising, no dysmorphism, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care glucose 4.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); ECG within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing management plan?

options.text: Admit for a minimum 24-hour period of continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and inpatient metabolic screen
Send home immediately with red-flag advice and a follow-up appointment with his general practitioner in a week
Perform full septic workup with lumbar puncture, empirical intravenous antibiotics and admission for 48 hours of observation
Observe with continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours, obtain pertussis PCR and ECG, and involve senior paediatrics before disposition
Arrange a home apnoea monitor before discharge and refer for outpatient echocardiography within 2 weeks

stem:
A 7-month-old boy is brought to your regional emergency department by his mother with 8 hours of intermittent crying episodes lasting minutes at a time, during which he draws his legs up and appears very distressed. Between episodes he has been lethargic and floppy on his mother's shoulder. He had two episodes of non-bilious vomiting and one soft stool that his mother describes as looking like dark red jam.

On examination he is pale and quiet between episodes with cool peripheries and capillary refill of three seconds. Abdomen is soft with a long thin lump palpable in the right upper quadrant. Bowel sounds are increased. Rectal examination reveals dark red mucus on the examining finger. He is otherwise well grown and fully immunised. A point-of-care ultrasound in the department shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant. He is haemodynamically stable after a single 20 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168/min post fluid, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes, long thin right upper quadrant mass, dark red mucus per rectum, increased bowel sounds, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant; venous blood gas within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue observation for another 4 hours with intravenous maintenance fluids alone because reduction may occur spontaneously
Prescribe oral ondansetron 2 mg with plain film abdominal radiography before considering any intervention today
Refer to general paediatrics for outpatient contrast enema imaging in the next few days after initial rehydration
Prepare for emergency laparotomy with primary bowel resection because ultrasound-confirmed intussusception is a surgical diagnosis
Arrange urgent radiology-led pneumatic (air) enema reduction under paediatric surgical cover once resuscitation is adequate

stem:
A previously well 3-year-old boy is brought to your rural emergency department by ambulance with a 12-hour illness of high fever, leg pain and vomiting. In the last 2 hours he has become increasingly floppy and pale and his mother has noticed several purple spots on his ankles that do not blanch. Retrieval to the tertiary paediatric centre has been requested and is estimated at 90 minutes.

On arrival he is grunting, mottled, with cold peripheries and capillary refill of 5 seconds. There is a non-blanching purpuric rash spreading on his lower limbs and abdomen with two large lesions greater than 2 cm across. Neck is soft and Brudzinski is negative. His weight is 15 kg. Point-of-care blood glucose is 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0). Intraosseous access has been obtained after failed IV attempts.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 96 percent on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 39.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mottled, cold peripheries, capillary refill 5 seconds, non-blanching purpuric rash with two lesions greater than 2 cm, grunting respirations
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.22, lactate 4.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-6.0); coagulation and FBC pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial antibiotic and dose to administer via the intraosseous line now?

options.text: Intraosseous ceftriaxone 100 mg per kilogram (maximum 4 g) as a single dose, given after a 20 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus
Intraosseous benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kilogram (maximum 3 g) as a single dose, then re-evaluate before further antibiotics
Intraosseous amoxicillin 50 mg per kilogram plus gentamicin 7 mg per kilogram as first-line antimicrobial regimen
Intraosseous vancomycin 15 mg per kilogram as monotherapy before any other antibiotic is started
Intraosseous cefotaxime 25 mg per kilogram as a single reduced dose because he is already in septic shock

stem:
A 12-day-old boy is brought to your regional emergency department by his parents with 2 days of poor feeding, vomiting and increasing sleepiness. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, discharged at day 3 after normal newborn screening bloodspots. He is exclusively breastfed with occasional formula top-ups. His parents describe him as normal until day 10.

On examination he is pale, floppy and mottled with poor tone. His anterior fontanelle is soft and mucous membranes are dry. Genitals appear normal male with descended testes and no obvious virilisation. His weight today is 3.0 kg, down from 3.4 kg at birth. Bedside investigations reveal sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5), venous pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-30) and lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2). No infection focus is identified after examination and initial cultures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Floppy, mottled, dry mucous membranes, normal male genitalia with descended testes, no ambiguity
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 6.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); venous glucose 2.4 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L (22-30); lactate 1.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Empirical intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg per kilogram and admit for full septic workup and observation over 24 hours
Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg immediately, 10 mL per kilogram normal saline bolus with 10 percent dextrose, and correction of hyperkalaemia
Intravenous fludrocortisone 0.1 mg as an initial single dose with intravenous normal saline maintenance over 24 hours
Intravenous insulin 0.05 units per kilogram per hour with 10 percent dextrose to lower the serum potassium before further therapy
Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 3 mL per kilogram as first-line correction of the severe hyponatraemia

subtopic_detail: Neonatal seizure with disconfirming metabolic finding
stem:
A term 36-hour-old girl is reviewed by you on the postnatal ward after nursing staff observed a 90-second episode of rhythmic left-sided facial twitching with bicycling limb movements. She was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated caesarean for breech presentation. Her mother has no medical history; there was no maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes or perinatal hypoxia (Apgars 9 and 9). Her mother is breastfeeding, with normal feed volumes so far.

On examination between episodes she is pink, alert and moving all four limbs symmetrically. Anterior fontanelle is soft. There is no rash. Head circumference is on the 50th centile. Point-of-care venous glucose is 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-5.5). Serum sodium is 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), venous ammonia 42 micromol/L (<50). Cerebrospinal fluid is bland with normal glucose and no organisms. A cranial ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148/min, blood pressure 68/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive between episodes, symmetrical limb movement, soft fontanelle, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.6-5.5); sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145); calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); magnesium 0.88 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); ammonia 42 mcmol/L (<50); CSF bland; cranial ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous phenobarbital 20 mg per kilogram loading dose without further metabolic testing today
Request an urgent magnetic resonance imaging scan of the brain looking for hypoxic ischaemic injury or cortical malformation
Administer a 100 mg intravenous pyridoxine trial with concurrent continuous electroencephalography monitoring
Request very-long-chain fatty acids and organic acids on plasma to screen for peroxisomal disorders as the priority test
Administer intravenous 10 percent dextrose 2 mL per kilogram bolus followed by 6 mg per kilogram per minute infusion for hypoglycaemia
